title: "probability basics"

## conditional probability & independence

- $P(A\mid B)$ is the probability of $A$ given that $B$ has occurred: $P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}$ for $P(B)>0$
- $A$ and $B$ are independent when knowing one tells you nothing about the other: $P(A\mid B)=P(A)$, equivalently $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$
- independence is an assumption to check, not a default — naive bayes relies on a (often wrong, still useful) assumption that features are independent given the class

## bayes' theorem

- bayes' theorem inverts a conditional probability: $P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{P(B\mid A)\,P(A)}{P(B)}$
- in modelling terms, with a hypothesis/class $h$ and observed data $d$: $P(h\mid d)=\dfrac{P(d\mid h)\,P(h)}{P(d)}$, read as posterior $\propto$ likelihood $\times$ prior
- $P(h)$ is the prior belief before seeing data, $P(d\mid h)$ is the likelihood of the data under that hypothesis, $P(d)$ is a normalising constant summed/integrated over all hypotheses, and $P(h\mid d)$ is the updated (posterior) belief
- naive bayes classifiers apply this directly: pick the class $c$ that maximises $P(c\mid x)\propto P(x\mid c)\,P(c)$, using the (naive) assumption that features of $x$ are conditionally independent given $c$

## random variables, expectation & variance

- a random variable maps outcomes to numbers; it is discrete (countable values, e.g. a class label) or continuous (e.g. a measurement)
- expectation is the probability-weighted average: $\mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_x x\,P(X=x)$ for discrete $X$, or $\int x\,f(x)\,dx$ for continuous $X$ with density $f$
- variance measures spread around the mean: $\operatorname{var}(X)=\mathbb{E}[(X-\mathbb{E}[X])^2]=\mathbb{E}[X^2]-\mathbb{E}[X]^2$
- expectation is linear — $\mathbb{E}[aX+bY]=a\mathbb{E}[X]+b\mathbb{E}[Y]$ — even when $X$ and $Y$ are dependent; this underlies the [bias-variance decomposition](../training-evaluation/bias-variance.qmd)

## common distributions

::: {.table-responsive tabindex="0"}

| distribution | models | typical use in ml |
|---|---|---|
| bernoulli | a single binary outcome (0/1) | the label in binary classification |
| binomial | number of successes in $n$ independent bernoulli trials | counts of successes/events |
| gaussian (normal) | continuous, symmetric, bell-shaped data | noise assumption behind least squares; many natural measurements |
| poisson | counts of rare events in a fixed interval | event-count data (e.g. mutations per sample) |

:::

- many models assume a distribution for the noise or the outcome — least squares implicitly assumes gaussian-distributed residuals, logistic regression assumes a bernoulli-distributed label; see [loss functions](../training-evaluation/loss-functions.qmd) for how this connects to maximum likelihood

## practical considerations

- a flat/uninformative prior lets the data dominate the posterior; a strong prior matters most when data is scarce
- the independence assumption behind naive bayes is usually false in a strict sense, but the classifier can still work well because only the relative ranking of $P(c\mid x)$ across classes needs to be right, not the exact probabilities
- check which distribution a model assumes before trusting its inferences — violating that assumption (e.g. skewed, heavy-tailed data treated as gaussian) can bias estimates and understate uncertainty
